title: Introduction to GPUs
learningGoals: Explain CPU vs GPU architecture and why GPUs suit massively parallel, data-parallel AI/ML work.
Describe the GPU as a co-processor: the host–device workflow and heterogeneous computing.
Explain CPU–GPU data transfer (RAM ↔ VRAM over PCIe / NVLink), why it's a bottleneck, and how to optimise it.
Explain the threading hierarchy: thread → block (programmer-defined) → grid, shared memory, SM, and the GPU "kernel".
Explain warps (NVIDIA, 32 threads) and wavefronts (AMD, 64), and calculate warp counts.
Compare SIMD vs SIMT, and explain branch divergence.
Estimate GPU vs CPU performance and list the factors: occupancy, memory access pattern, divergence, latency hiding.
sirStressed: "The hottest thing in the world: GPUs." You must be able to explain what GPUs are, how they differ from CPUs, and why they matter for AI.
A GPU kernel is a function that runs on the GPU. Don't confuse it with the OS kernel.

Thread, block and grid are generic terms. Warp and SM are NVIDIA terms (AMD: wavefront). A warp is a hardware execution group of 32, and blocks are logical groupings by the programmer. Numbering starts at 0.
Each SM has limited registers and shared memory, so an SM fits only some blocks at once.
Total time = transfer in + launch + compute + transfer out, so the CPU can win for small jobs.
Data movement is very important. "When you calculate, consider the time taken to move the data to and fro… If you reduce data movement, you're scoring very high." Optimisation is super important.
The Computing Systems assignment was live at this point (a student noted it unlocks only after you complete the course survey). AI tools may be used, but not for generating screenshots of output.
commonTraps: Thinking GPU cores are as powerful as CPU cores. They're many but simple.
Warp size: NVIDIA warp = 32; AMD wavefront = 64.
Block vs warp: the block is programmer-defined; the warp is hardware-defined.
Forgetting the data-transfer overhead (PCIe/NVLink). It's often the real bottleneck.
SIMD vs SIMT: SIMT gives each thread its own PC and registers, so it can branch.
"More threads always means faster." Occupancy, memory access, divergence and transfers decide.
Shared memory vs VRAM: shared memory = small, fast, on-chip, per block. VRAM = large, global, slower.
summary: CPU = few powerful cores for varied and control tasks. GPU = thousands of simple cores for the same operation on huge data. VRAM is GPU memory. Uses: AI/ML/DL, graphics and gaming, video, science, self-driving cars, GPU-as-a-Service.

Co-processor model (heterogeneous): the CPU = host (brain/manager); the GPU = device (specialist). Workflow: prepare in RAM → copy to VRAM → launch the kernel → copy results back. Parallelism requires independent tasks.
Transfers: PCIe (tens of GB/s) and NVLink (faster). Transfers are a bottleneck. Batch, keep data on the GPU, overlap, use PyTorch, TensorFlow or CuPy.

Hierarchy: thread (smallest unit) → block (programmer, shares shared memory) → grid (all blocks). Hardware: warp = 32 threads (NVIDIA) or wavefront = 64 (AMD), run on SMs (limited registers and shared memory).
Shared memory = fast on-chip memory, like a cache. VRAM = global and slow.
Kernel = a GPU function (CUDA). Global index = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x .
SIMD = one instruction on multiple data (rigid). SIMT = threads with their own PC and registers that can branch (modern GPUs). Divergence costs time.

Performance: occupancy, memory access pattern (coalesced), divergence, latency hiding (warp switching), throughput. Time ≈ operations ÷ effective throughput. 1M additions: CPU with 8 cores ≈ 125 ms vs GPU with 10k cores ≈ 0.1 ms (plus transfer).

Using the lecture's model, estimate the time to add two arrays of 2 million elements on an 8-core CPU (where 125,000 additions per core ≈ 125 ms) and on a GPU with 20,000 cores.
correctAnswers: CPU: 2,000,000 / 8 = 250,000 per core ≈ 250 ms (twice the lecture's 125 ms). GPU: 2,000,000 / 20,000 = 100 per core, the same per-core load as the lecture's example, so ≈ 0.1 ms, plus the RAM↔VRAM transfer time.

questions.prompt: A data scientist moves each training batch to the GPU, computes, copies the loss back to the CPU after every operation, and finds the GPU barely faster than the CPU. Explain why, and suggest two fixes.
correctAnswers: The time goes on CPU↔GPU data transfer over PCIe, not computation. Sending results back after every operation adds huge overhead. Fixes: keep the data and intermediate results on the GPU (copy back only at the end of an epoch or step), batch transfers, overlap transfer with computation, and use a framework such as PyTorch or TensorFlow that manages device memory.
questions.explanation: The time goes on CPU↔GPU data transfer over PCIe, not computation. Sending results back after every operation adds huge overhead. questions.prompt: Why does adding 2 to 10 million numbers suit a GPU, while running a word processor, a music player and a scanner together suits a CPU?
correctAnswers: Adding 2 to 10 million numbers is the same simple operation on independent data, which is perfect for thousands of simple GPU cores running in parallel (data parallelism). The word processor, music player and scanner are different, varied tasks with interrupts, I/O and complex control logic, which need the powerful general-purpose CPU cores and multitasking.
